core.text: A small family of nouns runs on the vowel *u*: **a 4th-declension noun (the u-pattern: manus, manus)**. The dictionary shows the pair *-us, -ūs*; the second form is the genitive (the 'of' form), and that long *-ūs* is what tells you the noun is 4th, not 2nd. Singular: *exercitus, exercitum, exercitūs, exercituī, exercitū*; plural: *exercitūs, exercitūs, exercituum, exercitibus, exercitibus*. Most are masculine — *exercitus* (army), *arcus* (bow), *passus* (pace), *metus* (fear), *impetus* (attack); *manus* (hand) is feminine; *cornū* (horn) is neuter. Latin name: dēclīnātiō quārta.
A declension is a family of nouns that share one set of endings. English has none; the nearest thing is the plural pattern *ox / oxen* against *box / boxes*.
Genitive singular -ūs marks the family: -us, -um, -ūs, -uī, -ū; plural -ūs, -ūs, -uum, -ibus, -ibus.

invented.en: The soldier holds his sword in his hand.

core.text: Both families have *-ibus* in the plural, and an *-us* nominative can belong to either (*tempus* is 3rd, *exercitus* 4th). The genitive settles it: *temporis* (3rd) against *exercitūs* (4th). The 2nd declension has *-us* too — *servus, servī* — but its genitive is *-ī*, never *-ūs*.

teach.title: What it does
teach.say: Most nouns you have met run on *a* (*puella*) or on *o* (*servus*). A small family runs on *u* instead, and each of its members is **a 4th-declension noun (the u-pattern: manus, manūs)**: *exercitus* (army), *manus* (hand), *arcus* (bow), *metus* (fear), *impetus* (attack), *passus* (pace). The dictionary always prints one as a pair, *exercitus, exercitūs*.

check.ask: Which word here belongs to the u-family?

teach.title: Subject -us, object -um
teach.say: One cell at a time. The nominative (the subject form) ends in *-us*: *exercitus*. The accusative (the object form) ends in *-um*: *exercitum*, *manum*, *arcum*. So far it looks exactly like *servus, servum*.

show.say: exercitus / exercitum — so far it looks exactly like servus / servum

check.ask: Fill the subject cell and the object cell of *exercitus*.

teach.title: The genitive -ūs is the family's mark
teach.say: Here is where it stops looking like *servus*. The genitive (the 'of' form) ends in a long *-ūs*: *exercitūs*, of the army. That one cell is what the dictionary prints, and it is what tells you the noun belongs to this family and not to another.

show.say: exercitūs — a long -ūs, where servus would have -ī

check.ask: Give the genitive (the 'of' form) of *exercitus* — the one cell that proves the family.

teach.title: The last two singular endings: -uī and -ū
teach.say: Two cells more. The dative (the 'to/for' form) is *-uī*: *exercituī*, to the army. The ablative (the 'by/with/from' form) is a bare long *-ū*: *manū*, in his hand. Both keep the family's *u* in plain sight.

show.say: exercituī / exercitū — both keep the family's u in plain sight

check.ask: Give the dative (the 'to/for' form) and the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form) of *exercitus*.

teach.title: The plural: -ūs, -uum, -ibus
teach.say: The plural subject and object are both *-ūs* (*exercitūs*, *manūs*), the genitive is *-uum* (*exercituum*), and the dative and ablative are *-ibus* (*manibus*). The neuters *genū* (knee) and *cornū* (horn) take *-ua* instead: *genua*.

check.ask: Fill the three plural cells of *exercitus*: the subject one, the 'of' one, and the 'to/for' one.

teach.title: Telling it from the other -us nouns
teach.say: Three families own an *-us* nominative, and only the genitive settles which is which: *servus, servī* is 2nd; *corpus, corporis* is 3rd; *exercitus, exercitūs* is 4th. *-ibus* in the plural is shared with the 3rd, so it proves nothing on its own. Learn each noun with its genitive.

check.ask: Amīcus servī venit, sed dux ___ abest. The 'of' form is what proves the family. (exercitus)

more.text: *Domus* (house) mixes the 4th and the 2nd: *domus, domum, domūs, domuī, domō*; plural *domūs, domōs, domuum* (or *domōrum*), *domibus*. It keeps three special forms: *domī* (at home), *domum* (homewards), *domō* (from home).

The learner's notes (week 12): the dative and ablative plural is *-ibus*, not the *-ubus* you might expect (the old *-ubus* survives in a few words such as *artubus*, *tribubus*); the nominative singular *-us* is short, while the genitive singular and the nominative and accusative plural have long *-ūs*. Almost all are masculine; the feminine exceptions such as *manus* are flagged in the vocabulary. The rare neuters (*cornū*, *genū* knee) run *-ū, -ū, -ūs, -ū, -ū; -ua, -ua, -uum, -ibus, -ibus*.

Ørberg (chapter XII) declines *exercitus* and lists *arcus, passus, equitātus* (cavalry), *impetus, metus, versus* (line of verse), with feminine *manus*. *Mīlle passūs* — a thousand paces — is the Roman mile; *duo mīlia passuum* shows the genitive plural.
